newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Queensland coal ports re-open in Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Queensland coal ports re-open in Australia.

text.p: Shipment of coal through cylone-battered ports in the Australian state of Queensland is resuming on Thursday as heavy seas start to abate.
The Hay Point terminal, which ships 25 million tonnes of coal a year, re-opened Thursday morning, port officials told Reuters.
Four ships were waiting to be loaded and it would probably take three days to clear them, officials said.
The Gladstone bulk coal port loaded a single vessel on Wednesday, an official there said.
This vessel, bound for South Korea, had now left port. Its early loading was possible because it was already partly laden with coal from another Australian port, the official said.
A full resumption of loading activities at Gladstone, which ships 15 million tonnes of coal a year, would begin later on Thursday, the official said.
Two vessels were at berth while a further three were waiting outside the berth area, the official said.
The two ships at berth would sail on Friday.

Hay Point and Gladstone ship coal from Central Queensland Coal Associates, a consortium of the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP), Japan's Mitsubishi Development Pty Ltd, the Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP) and QCT Resources Ltd.
The coal port at Dalrymple Bay, adjacent to Hay Point and used by a variety of Queensland producers, had not yet been re-opened, an official said at 00.00 GMT.
An examination was in progress at the time to see if the port could be re-opened, the official said.
Vessels could be loaded quickly if the port re-opened. If it did not re-open Thursday it would probably re-open on Friday, the official said.
It was not immediately known how many vessels were waiting to be loaded at Dalrymple Bay, which exports about 26 million tonnes of coal a year.
Australia exports almost A$8 billion worth of coal a year to Asia, Europe and South America through its main Queensland ports.
Cyclone Justin was expected to move very little during the next 24 hours, the weather bureau said on Thursday.
It was expected to hover off the Queensland coast over the next two days with little change in its intensity, which remained reduced from earlier this week, bureau officials said.
